# Non-Uniqueness of Smooth Solutions of the Navier–Stokes Equations from Critical Data

Matei P. Coiculescu∗and Stan Palasek†

March 18, 2025

## Abstract

We consider the Cauchy problem for the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations in dimension three and construct initial data in the critical space BMO−1 from which there exist two distinct global solutions, both smooth for all t > 0. One consequence of this construction is the sharpness of the celebrated small data global well-posedness result of Koch and Tataru. This appears to be the first example of non-uniqueness for the Navier–Stokes equations with data at the critical regularity. The proof is based on a non-uniqueness mechanism proposed by the second author in the context of the dyadic Navier–Stokes equations.

## 1 Introduction

Consider the initial value problem for the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations on T3 or R3: ∂tu −ν∆u + u · ∇u + ∇p = 0

where the given initial data U0(x) is divergence-free, and u(x, t) and p(x, t) are the unknown velocity and pressure fields. By rescaling, we assume without loss of generality that ν = 1. Initiated in 1934 by the pioneering work of Leray [40], there is now a well-developed theory of local well-posedness of (1.1) from initial data in many reasonable classes of functions, as well as global well-posedness from data that is sufficiently small in certain scale-invariant norms; see, for instance, [38] for an extensive survey. The strongest result in this direction is the following well-known theorem of Koch and Tataru [37]:

Critical spaces are a natural setting for the questions we consider because they are at the threshold of the well-posedness theory; there are many theorems to the effect that certain classes of critical solutions are well-behaved [26, 28, 4, 5, 12, 2, 44, 43, 42, 39, 16, 32]. To our knowledge, Theorem 1.2 is the first ill-posedness result in a critical space strong enough to support well-posedness for small data. Moreover, it appears to be the first example of non-uniqueness for the Navier–Stokes equations from data in any critical space that does not rely on the presence of an external force. See §1.2 for a comparison of our solutions to those constructed previously in the literature.

Remark 1.5. Let us emphasize that the solutions constructed in Theorem 1.2 are not in the Leray–Hopf class due to the fact that the initial velocity is not in L2(T3). The construction here uses a simplified version of the mechanism proposed by the second author in [47] and this simplification requires the data to have infinite energy. If the full mechanism from [47] could be implemented, we expect it would yield solutions of (1.1) in a similar class as those of Jia and ˇSver´ak [34, 35] (but without exact self-similarity), namely Leray–Hopf solutions

After preparation of the manuscript, Cheskidov, Zeng, and Zhang posted a preprint [19] in which they use convex integration to construct wild weak solutions of the Navier–Stokes and MHD from any H 1 2 initial data. This is an interesting contribution that implies the lack of weak-strong uniqueness of dissipative solutions. We wish to emphasize that the solutions produced in [19] do not overlap with Theorem 1.2 at all; while they have the advantage that the data is in L2(R3), they do not appear to possess any further regularity for t > 0, nor does the energy inequality hold. The present paper is concerned with the question of well-posedness of mild solutions, which is orthogonal to the setting treated in [19]. This can be seen from the fact that they construct distinct solutions even for small data in H 1 2 (R3).

The spaces B−1+3/p p,q are critical for the three-dimensional Navier–Stokes equations for all p, q ∈[1, ∞], although they primarily play a role in the negative regularity regime p > 3. ### 1.2 Known Approaches towards Non-Uniqueness

Up to this point, there have been two strategies for producing non-unique solutions to (1.1) and other equations of fluid dynamics. Here we briefly summarize the state of the art.

### 1.2.1 Convex Integration

Inspired by Nash’s C1 isometric embedding theorem [46], De Lellis and Sz´ekelyhidi introduced convex integration to the field of mathematical fluid dynamics in their seminal papers [25, 24]. Whereas for the Euler equations these methods produced essentially sharp results (culminating, for instance, in the resolution of Onsager’s conjecture [33]), for the Navier–Stokes equations there remain some persistent gaps between the regularity reached by convex integration schemes and the known well-posedness results. This area has been highly active so we refer the reader to [10] for a more thorough survey. The first example of non-unique weak solutions of (1.1) was constructed in the space CtHϵ x for ϵ > 0 small in the breakthrough work of Buckmaster and Vicol [9]. For comparison, the critical space in this scale in dimension three is CtH1/2 x , and Leray–Hopf solutions

additionally lie in L2 t H1 x. Tao [51] observed that one can reach regularity CtH

Among the subsequent convex integration constructions following [9], for instance [7, 41, 17, 18], the sharpest in terms of the scaling of the space are those of Cheskidov and Luo: first in [17], they construct solutions in L2−ϵ t L∞ x (Rn) for n ≥2 and all ϵ > 0. Later in [18], they exhibit solutions in the space CtL2−ϵ x (R2), where ϵ > 0 can be taken arbitrarily small. For comparison, L2 t L∞ x and L∞ t Ln x are critical in dimension n; thus, their solutions can get arbitrarily close to certain critical spaces on the Prodi–Serrin– Ladyzhenskaya scale and possess some additional favorable properties outside of a small set of times. Unfortunately, convex integration at or above critical regularity appears out of reach. Indeed, the nonlinearity must be at least as large as the Laplacian in order for the error correction to function, so there is no room to lose anything during the iteration. Moreover, convex integration is only known to be applicable in settings where the solution space has flexibility, which is certainly not the case for solutions that immediately regularize like the ones in Theorem 1.2, nor (one might expect) for Leray–Hopf solutions, which exhibit weak-strong uniqueness. There are additional difficulties related to finding sufficiently intermittent building blocks which present an obstacle to, among other things, proving the sharpness of the full Prodi–Serrin–Ladyzhenskaya scale.

### 1.2.2 The Jia–ˇSver´ak Program

The other known strategy for demonstrating non-uniqueness was set forth by Jia and ˇSver´ak in [34, 35]. They propose to consider (1.1) in self-similar coordinates ξ = x/t1/2, τ = log t with the ansatz u(t, x) = t−1/2U(ξ, τ). Thus the question of non-uniqueness for u at t = 0 is transferred to U at τ = −∞, which would be settled if one can find a steady solution U(ξ, τ) = U(ξ) that is nonlinearly unstable in the self-similar dynamics. This scenario seems plausible in light of compelling numerical evidence by Guillod and ˇSver´ak [31]. Recently, Albritton, Bru´e, and Colombo [1] used this framework to construct non-unique Leray–Hopf solutions to the forced Navier–Stokes equations by building a profile U out of the unstable vortex constructed by Vishik in [53, 54]. The force is necessary for their construction because U does not satisfy the Navier–Stokes in self-similar coordinates. Removing the force appears extremely difficult because the only suspected unstable self-similar profile is the one numerically discovered in [31]. It follows that one would have to verify spectral properties of the equation linearized around a numerical profile.

### 1.3 Strategy of the Proof

The non-uniqueness mechanism that leads to Theorem 1.2 is based on the one proposed by the second author in the context of the Obukhov dyadic model in [47], with certain simplifications to make the construction feasible in the full PDE setting. Let us now sketch the strategy of the proof, neglecting some details for the purpose of the exposition.

### 1.3.1 Non-Uniqueness Mechanism

The initial data3 is constructed as a lacunary series U0 = P k≥0 V 0 k where each V 0 k is (approximately) localized in Fourier space to a band around |ξ| = Nk, with Nk a rapidly growing sequence of frequency scales. The essence of the construction is the following claim: there exists a choice of the (V 0 k )k∈N such that at each frequency level k, there exist two evolutions forward in time that are consistent with (1.1), up to a small error:

• The Heat-Dominated Flow: let vk(x, t) be the flow of the data under the heat equation, namely ∂tvk −∆vk = l.o.t.

vk|t=0 = V 0 k (1.3)

where we add some lower order terms as a matter of convenience. Clearly ∥vk(t)∥L∞ decays exponentially on the time scale N−2 k .

• The Inverse Cascade-Dominated Flow: let vk(x, t) be the flow of the data under the equation ∂tvk + P∼NkP div vk+1 ⊗vk+1 = 0

vk|t=0 = V 0 k (1.4)

Taking for granted the assertions made so far (which, indeed, most of the paper will be occupied with justifying), we can write down two distinct approximate solutions of (1.1) with data U0 = P k≥0 V 0 k :

v(1) := v0 + v1 + v2 + v3 + · · · and v(2) := v0 + v1 + v2 + v3 + · · · . (1.5)

The distinctness is immediate from the fact that vk and vk have different decay rates. Let us give a more heuristic description of how the non-uniqueness arises. Fixing k ≥1, one should interpret (1.4) as asserting that V 0 k+1 is capable of using its nonlinear selfinteraction to “annihilate” the mode below that has initial data V 0 k , and this annihilation occurs on time scale N−2 k+1. Likewise, V 0 k is capable of annihilating the mode at V 0 k−1 on time scale N−2 k . However, these two events are incompatible because the kth mode would vanish on a time scale (i.e., N−2 k+1) much shorter than the time it needs to act on vk−1 (i.e., N−2 k ). Thus, if V 0 k is in fact annihilated by V 0 k+1 (i.e., its continuation vk(t) satisfies (1.4)), then there are no nonlinear dynamics to act on V 0 k−1, which then evolves as the heat-dominated flow vk−1(t) according to (1.3). The conclusion of the discussion above is that these dynamics are only self-consistent if (1.3) and (1.4) occur at alternating sequences of k’s, which justifies the choice (1.5). The non-uniqueness then is a consequence of the fact that (1.3) can occur at either every odd k or every even k.

### 1.3.2 Structure of the Principal Part

An obvious difficulty is that even if we can arrange (1.3)–(1.4), there remains a plethora of nonlinear interactions between the vk’s and vk’s that need to be small for us to claim these as approximate solutions. It turns out that if the data is chosen appropriately, the terms appearing in (1.3)–(1.4) are the only ones that are non-perturbative. ### 1.4 Plan of the Paper

In §2, we state some of the basic Littlewood–Paley theory and related estimates (§2.2–2.3) and introduce some of the key parameters that go into the construction (§2.4). In §3 we build the data U0 and the leading parts v(i) of the solutions: first we construct the Mikado building blocks for the initial data and prove estimates on the supports (§3.1); then we run the iterative procedure to construct the initial data and prove estimates (§3.2); followed by construction of the leading parts of the two distinct solutions forward in time (§3.3). §4 is concerned with constructing the perturbation w(i) that will correct the principal parts v(i): first we estimate the residuals F (i) that are to be corrected (§4.1); then we construct the semigroup S(i) of the Navier–Stokes linearized around the principal parts v(i) (§4.2); and finally we construct the perturbations with a fixed point argument (§4.3). In §5, we complete the proof of Theorem 1.2, proving that the two solutions constructed attain the initial data and are distinct. Appendices A–C give some technical tools used in the proofs.
